filesystem_writes_scope: This action creates, modifies and deletes no file and no file content. Two side effects it cannot avoid are reported rather than covered by that claim. (1) The shell spools the embedded program to an unlinked temporary file before the interpreter starts, because the control plane pipes one self-contained script over SSH and a here-document above the pipe-buffer size is spooled rather than piped; that file holds the program text, not host data, and does not outlive the shell. (2) `du` reads every directory it traverses, and under the kernel's default `relatime` -- or `strictatime` -- the kernel updates those directories' ACCESS TIMES as a result. That is a metadata write caused by reading, so it cannot be avoided while measuring at all, and whether it happens is a property of the host's mount options rather than of this action: inventory.volume.atime reports the measured policy and directory_atime_writes_suppressed is true only under noatime or nodiratime. No file content, size, name or ownership is changed either way. (3) PostgreSQL itself may append to its server log for this action's connections and read-only statements, as its logging configuration directs (log_connections, log_disconnections, log_statement, log_duration, log_min_duration_statement, auto_explain); that is the database server's write, not measured here and not covered by the flag below. filesystem_writes_performed reports that metadata write and nothing else: true once a du traversal has started on a filesystem mounted relatime or strictatime, false under noatime or nodiratime or when no traversal ran, and null when the mount policy could not be read.

inventory.dead_tuple_bytes_meaning: estimated dead space inside each relation: reusable by that relation's own future rows once routine dead-row cleanup has run, and not returned to the filesystem. Returning it needs a full table rewrite, which takes an exclusive lock and temporary space for the new copy.

index_statistics_window.note: stats_reset is pg_stat_database's database-wide value. A single index or table may have been reset independently with pg_stat_reset_single_table_counters, which zeroes idx_scan without changing this timestamp, and PostgreSQL records no per-index reset time. Treat each index's observation window as unknown: a zero idx_scan is not evidence that an index is unused, and must not on its own justify dropping one.

summary.method: accounted_bytes = operating_database_bytes + other_databases_bytes + wal_bytes + wal_summaries_bytes + wal_archive_status_bytes + current PostgreSQL temporary-directory bytes, the three WAL figures read in one closing statement; unaccounted_bytes = volume_used_bytes - accounted_bytes. largest_unaccounted_directories is numerically non-overlapping across its retained rows: each row reports its own total minus the totals of its scanned children, the measured PostgreSQL data-directory size is subtracted from the deepest scanned directory that contains it, and the data directory itself is excluded. Directories UNDER it are not all excluded: only the accounted ones are, so those an accounted figure does not cover (global, pg_xact, pg_multixact, pg_stat, pg_stat_tmp, pg_xlog, replication-slot state, base/ entries that are not live database directories, relative log files, and files at the data directory's own root) appear as rows flagged inside_data_directory. No row counts the database twice, and no row counts another row's bytes. Rows outside the data directory sum to non_database_directory_bytes; rows inside it sum to unaccounted_inside_data_directory_bytes. Some of the latter must never be deleted -- they are location evidence, not reclaim suggestions. The depth-2 root stream is bounded; retained ancestors keep numerical byte coverage, but when records_omitted_by_cap is nonzero the receipt does not claim complete path ownership or enumeration. Its omitted_record_cumulative_bytes is diagnostic only because ancestor and descendant records may overlap, and it is never a candidate or uncertainty. The base/ rows come from postgres_base_directory_breakdown, a depth-1 du scan that identifies live database directories by OID, so each entry that is NOT a live database is named by path. They are NOT base/'s du total minus the pg_database_size totals: du measures allocated filesystem blocks and pg_database_size sums each entry's st_size, so that subtraction reported ordinary per-file block rounding as orphaned storage. That difference is database_size_metric_difference_bytes, which is two tools measuring the same files differently and is not reclaimable. When the breakdown is unavailable (reason recorded there) no base/ row is emitted. THIS RECEIPT DOES NOT CLAIM THE CANDIDATES BALANCE EXACTLY, and it is worth saying why, because an exact claim would look stronger. Every figure here is measured at a different moment from the one it is compared with: df is a single instant, du is a walk lasting minutes, and the SQL queries fall between them, while the database writes and WAL is created and recycled throughout. There is no instant at which all of these could be read together, so an exact identity could only ever be defended by adding one correction term per way the measurements can disagree -- and each such term is another pair of readings to disagree about. The question this action exists to answer does not need it: an operator deciding what to reclaim needs to know which large things on the volume are not the database, and how precisely that is known. So candidate_shortfall_bytes is unaccounted_bytes_at_directory_scan minus candidate_total_bytes -- how much of the figure the listed directories do not explain -- and measurement_uncertainty_bytes is the summed width of every window involved, itemised in measurement_uncertainty_terms: the volume's movement across the window and across the root scan, the PGDATA and base/ brackets, the direct pg_wal PGDATA-walk-to-window-close width, the database total's movement, df against du (filesystem_minus_directory_scan_bytes), and du's allocated blocks against pg_database_size's st_size sums (database_size_metric_difference_bytes). candidates_account_for_unaccounted_within_uncertainty is whether the shortfall fits inside that width. None of those terms is storage anyone can free; they are how precisely the two sides are known. A shortfall LARGER than the uncertainty is a different matter and fails the operation: it means the listed directories genuinely do not explain the figure, which is what a large directory missing from the scan looks like. That comparison is only made when candidate_list_complete is true. An unavailable base breakdown removes base/'s rows from the list entirely, root-stream truncation prevents complete path attribution, and a contributing scan accepted after vanished-file diagnostics may have missed a renamed file (candidate_list_degraded_scans). Each condition is named in candidate_list_incomplete_reasons, and makes the verdict null -- not asserted, not disproved -- while the shortfall and uncertainty are still reported. Path attribution follows du, which counts a file with several hard links once, under whichever link its walk reaches first (hard_linked_files_attributed_to_one_path): a candidate's bytes are where du found them, not proof that deleting that path alone frees them, because another link elsewhere keeps the blocks allocated. Check link counts before reclaiming anything. The du scan covers the whole filesystem that holds the data directory, not only the PostgreSQL volume subdirectory. filesystem_minus_directory_scan_bytes is volume_used_bytes_at_directory_scan minus directory_scan_root_bytes -- the df reading taken immediately after that same scan, NOT volume_used_bytes, which is the closing reading that unaccounted_bytes uses because the database and WAL figures it subtracts are also closing figures. Pairing the scan with the closing reading would charge every byte written or freed by the intervening SQL to this residual, which is the same category the residual measures and so could not be told apart from it. df reports filesystem space and du estimates space used by files, so this gap is filesystem metadata, blocks held by deleted-but-open files, and any files hidden beneath a mount point below the scan root (du -x cannot see under a mount, while df still counts those blocks; see filesystem_minus_directory_scan_may_include_files_hidden_beneath_mounts) -- but only beyond filesystem_minus_directory_scan_uncertainty_bytes, which is how much the volume moved while the root walk was running. df is one instant and du is a traversal, so a sibling changing during the walk leaves its earlier or partly-observed size in directory_scan_root_bytes; a residual no larger than that width is ordinary movement rather than metadata or a deleted-but-open file, and is not flagged. Reserved blocks are NOT a cause: they explain size minus (used + available) because they remain free while being unavailable to ordinary users, so they never enter `used`; changing the reserved-block percentage cannot close this residual. Apart from files hidden beneath mount points -- which ARE directory contents, reachable only by unmounting and so invisible to this read-only scan -- the gap is not directory usage and cannot be reclaimed by deleting a directory. non_database_drill_down names the directory that owns the non-database usage, which a single bounded-depth scan from the root cannot do: GNU du shows directories at most N levels below the scanned root, so a depth-2 scan from / emits /var/lib but never /var/lib/docker
